title: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
desc: Finds stronger evidence for speed and cost than consistent quality, with grounding unable to remove probabilistic error.

kps.k: The cluster frames legal AI primarily as a copilot: it may assist information-intensive work, but humans retain judgment, supervision and accountability.
kps.d: Generative AI can support research, summarisation, document and contract review, due diligence, translation, compliance, drafting and administration. Existing professional duties—competence, diligence, candour, confidentiality and supervision—continue to govern its use. Lawyers remain responsible for legal advice and work product; judges retain decision-making authority; and agentic systems require meaningful human supervision. Some sources reject AI-generated legal briefing under current conditions, while another predicts that competence standards may eventually require careful use of sufficiently reliable AI.

qs.q: Although the ABA Model Rules were not written to address specific technologies, they are comprehensive enough to permit the responsible and ethical use of generative AI tools in legal practice.
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: “A lawyer’s                                         professional judgment cannot be delegated to [G]enerative                                         AI and remains the lawyer’s responsibility at all times.
qs.a: Formal Opinion 2024-5 — Ethical Obligations of Lawyers and Law Firms Relating to the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Measured benefits are task-specific and stronger for speed and cost than for consistently improved legal quality.
kps.d: Comparisons report that selected legal AI tools matched or outperformed lawyers on document summarisation, transcript analysis, data extraction, chronology generation and aspects of contract review. A legal-aid pilot reported an average 50% efficiency increase across participant-identified beneficial uses, but the measure was self-reported and selected for helpful applications. Contract-review studies reported large time and cost advantages, including one comparison at 0.03% of human cost. These findings do not establish superiority across legal practice: quality results remain mixed, legal automation predates generative AI, and reduced task-specific development cost may be a clearer advance than accuracy. Adoption data, demonstrations, vendor claims and forecasts do not independently prove effectiveness.

qs.q: *All four tools *outperformed the lawyers in the summarisation of documents and the analysis of transcripts, and Harvey Assistant, the platform developed by the eponymous legal technology start-up, even outperformed the lawyers in three additional areas – data extraction, the generation of chronologies, and document review and analysis.
qs.a: The Future of the Legal Profession: A Shared Vision — Opening Address at the Legal Profession Symposium 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Beneficial Use Cases      As discussed further below, across the uses in our companion case database, pilot participants reported an increase in efficiency of an av- erage of 50% on a wide range of tasks.
qs.a: Generative AI and Legal Aid: Results from a Field Study and 100 Use Cases to Bridge the Access to Justice Gap · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Evaluation must distinguish information processing from judgment-intensive legal work.
kps.d: Classification, extraction and some retrieval or summarisation tasks often permit comparison with reference labels or lawyer-produced answers. Advocacy, strategy and legal drafting may have several defensible formulations rather than one correct output, while even ostensibly objective information-processing tasks can contain ambiguity. Performance on a narrow benchmark therefore does not establish reliability for case-specific advice, substantive filings, prediction or other discretionary work. Evaluation should use representative tasks, relevant jurisdictions and criteria suited to the legal function, including net time to reach an acceptable quality level.

qs.q: We analyze three broad uses of AI in the legal domain: (i) tasks involving information processing, such as summarization or legal information retrieval; (ii) tasks involving creativity, reasoning, or judgment, such as preparing legal filings; and (iii) tasks involving predictions about the future, such as criminal risk prediction as well as predicting the outcomes of court decisions.
qs.a: Promises and pitfalls of artificial intelligence for legal applications · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Although you do not have to have full knowledge of the inner workings of a tool, consider the claims the provider is making about it and assess the evidence and benchmarks they use to demonstrate the tool’s capabilities.
qs.a: Generative AI: the essentials · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Probabilistic generation creates a substantive verification problem that grounding and legal databases reduce but do not remove.
kps.d: Generative models produce plausible text rather than independently validate legal meaning, authority or context. They may fabricate cases, quotations or facts; misstate genuine decisions; use stale or foreign law; omit decisive arguments; or combine accurate material into a false conclusion. Reported hallucination estimates vary sharply by tool and task: one account cites 17%–34% for tested commercial legal tools, subject to access limitations, while separate Stanford research reported at least 75% for specified general-purpose models answering questions about courts’ core rulings. These figures are not interchangeable or generalisable to all legal AI. Retrieval-augmented generation and curated databases can improve grounding, but retrieval omissions, outdated collections, misunderstood prompts and generation errors persist. Court sanctions incidents demonstrate the consequences of failed verification rather than model-wide error rates.

qs.q: “Hallucinations” It is important for lawyers to understand that language-driven generative AI is not a search engine with drafting features, but is instead a prediction engine that simply attempts to predict – word by word – an answer to a prompt.
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Effective verification requires qualified, independent review, but its cost and feasibility remain disputed.
kps.d: A responsible reviewer must compare output with authoritative sources, confirm that authorities exist and remain good law, verify quotations and attributed propositions, check jurisdiction and currency, assess analytical completeness and bias, and adapt the result to the client or case. Asking a generative system to confirm its own answer does not meet that standard, and discovered inaccuracies may trigger correction and notification duties. Advocates expect review still to yield net savings on suitable tasks; critics argue that proposition-by-proposition checking can erase those gains. Inexperienced lawyers may lack the legal knowledge needed to review efficiently, while persuasive output and workload pressure can produce verification drift even when users know the rules.

kps.k: Courts and regulators agree on human responsibility but diverge over disclosure, certification and prohibited uses.
kps.d: Regimes range from ordinary professional obligations and context-dependent disclosure to accuracy certificates, identification of AI-drafted passages and outright restrictions. Critics argue that broad disclosure rules conflate high-risk outsourcing of reasoning and drafting with lower-risk editing or brainstorming, become difficult to apply as AI enters ordinary software, and create fragmented compliance burdens. Supporters treat disclosure and certification as safeguards for provenance and accountability. Task-specific guidance increasingly permits uses such as chronologies, summaries, briefs and draft submissions subject to review, while restricting AI-generated witness evidence, expert content, autonomous filings and adjudication. Lawyers and court users must therefore check current local rules rather than assume a uniform standard.

qs.q: Judicial Responses to AI Judges at all levels of the judicial system across the country have issued dozens of judicial AI standing orders, imposing widely varying requirements on lawyers’ use of AI.
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: 5) Disclosing GenAI use You do not need to disclose use of a GenAI chatbot as a matter of course – unless asked by the court or tribunal.
qs.a: Guidelines for Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Courts and Tribunals — Lawyers · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: Accuracy controls alone are insufficient because confidentiality, bias, evidence integrity, billing and governance create distinct risks.
kps.d: Sensitive client information may be retained, reused or exposed when entered into unsuitable tools, requiring controlled environments, contractual review, access restrictions and, where necessary, anonymisation or non-use. Bias can arise from training data, system design and sycophancy, so users cannot presume neutrality. Deepfakes and concealed prompt instructions create evidentiary and cybersecurity threats beyond textual hallucination. Billing guidance generally permits charging for actual prompting, review and editing, not for hypothetical time saved by AI. Organisational controls include approved-tool lists, vendor due diligence, role-based access, staff training, audit trails, records of prompts and outputs, incident reporting, insurance review and periodic policy revision.

qs.q: Therefore, lawyers        should refrain from entering any personal, conﬁdential or other data related to the client        into the user interface of the GenAI, for example as prompts/queries, unless there are        appropriate safeguards in place.
qs.a: CCBE Guide on the Use of Generative AI by Lawyers · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: • Implement data access controls and apply sensitivity labels,                                                                                 restricting GenAI access to use only the information each user is                                                                                 authorised to view based on their role and responsibilities.
qs.a: Guide for Using Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Legal Sector · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Access-to-justice claims present a trade-off between broader assistance and users’ limited ability to verify legal output.
kps.d: Conversational systems could offer continuous help with issue spotting, translation, intake, forms, document preparation, court navigation and small claims, and courts and public-interest organisations have deployed early chatbots. This mechanism could reduce information and resource barriers, but the evidence does not show that AI has closed the justice gap or improved case outcomes. Self-represented users often lack legal knowledge, prompting skill and database access, making confident errors especially difficult to detect. Bad output can damage their cases, generate meritless filings and shift verification costs to courts and opposing parties. The policy dispute asks whether restrictive unauthorized-practice rules protect vulnerable users or suppress useful assistance. A middle position favours purpose-built and rigorously evaluated systems, authoritative sources, privacy safeguards, accessible design and escalation to human help.

qs.q: A  recent survey found that low-income Americans did not receive any or enough legal help for 92%  of their civil legal problems.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations of the New York State Bar Association Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (April 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: The ability of chatbots to follow natural language directions means laypeople can use them to perform information-processing tasks, such as translation or getting pointers to relevant legal rules.
qs.a: Promises and pitfalls of artificial intelligence for legal applications · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The practical implication is selective, risk-based adoption rather than uniform embrace or avoidance.
kps.d: Lower-risk starting points include input-grounded summarisation, translation, plain-language rewriting, brainstorming, administrative drafting and closed-corpus review. Higher-risk applications include case-specific advice, unfamiliar legal research, substantive advocacy, autonomous agentic workflows, witness or expert evidence and decisions affecting rights. Organisations should calibrate oversight to consequences, user expertise, tool design and reversibility; pilot on representative work; measure quality as well as net time and cost; and update controls as products change. Training should cover prompting, source verification, bias detection and when not to use AI, while preserving the independent research and reasoning through which junior lawyers develop evaluative competence.

qs.q: Lower-risk tasks where user-provided data or                      inputs limit hallucination risk      Pilot participants found beneficial use cases for lower-risk tasks where the input data grounds the AI model and limits the risk of hal- lucinations.
qs.a: Generative AI and Legal Aid: Results from a Field Study and 100 Use Cases to Bridge the Access to Justice Gap · Academia · 2025

qs.q: In a world where high performance generative AI tools are common, the most effective attorneys will not be those who use AI the most, but rather will be those who use it judiciously and carefully while also knowing when not to use it.
qs.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Practice of Law: Impact, Opportunities, and Risks · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources accept the proposition’s core: legal GenAI is principally an assistive copilot; evidence is stronger for task-specific speed and cost savings than for consistent quality; probabilistic errors persist despite legal databases and retrieval-augmented generation; and qualified humans retain verification, judgment and accountability. They materially develop that proposition by explaining why verification fails in practice—through automation bias, verification drift, time pressure, limited AI and legal literacy, and inexperienced lawyers’ difficulty evaluating work in unfamiliar areas—and by proposing concrete responses such as process-focused legal education, independent first attempts, empirical task-specific evaluation, certification, sanctions and targeted restrictions. Internal variation concerns emphasis rather than overall direction. Some sources foreground measurable or participant-reported gains in lower-risk work, while others argue proposition-by-proposition checking may undercut those gains. Access-to-justice scholarship sees potential for drafting and court navigation but stresses that self-represented users have weaker verification capacity. Regulatory scholarship disagrees over disclosure and prohibition, generally preferring either existing professional duties or complementary safeguards. A more optimistic strand predicts improving tools or eventual competence duties to use them, while one source considers hallucinations increasingly straightforward to minimise and redirects attention to deeper cognitive evaluation problems. Several claims about adoption, quality, displacement and access remain exploratory or prospective, and the Brazilian-courts study does not provide enough evidence to resolve the proposition’s verification-cost question. These sources are a curated selection and should not be treated as representative of academic or research opinion generally.

qs.q: Alternatively, as explained by verification drift, the risks are known but the persuasiveness of GenAI outputs when combined with time and resource pressures leads to risk management steps being foregone.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analysis, consultancy and press sources accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that legal AI is best treated as a copilot whose practical value depends on human verification and accountability. The sources commonly emphasise concrete consequences of unchecked output—fabricated authorities, sanctions, non-meritorious filings and possible breaches of tribunal rules—rather than offering systematic comparisons of quality, speed or net verification cost. Collectively, they materially extend the proposition by moving governance beyond lawyers’ own use: one loss-prevention source recommends documented client warnings about uploading privileged or confidential material and policies for recording or transcribing client conversations. There is meaningful internal variation. The loss-prevention source focuses on firm controls, confidentiality and tribunal compliance; one press account illustrates direct verification duties through a sanctions incident; and another presents the access-to-justice tension, recognising possible assistance for self-represented litigants while warning that easier generation and filing can facilitate legally baseless or harmful litigation. These accounts are largely incident-based and cautionary, so they reinforce the risk and governance dimensions more strongly than the cluster’s claims about measured efficiency or verification costs. As a curated selection, they should not be treated as representative of all market analysts, consultancies or press sources.

qs.q: “Just like a law firm would have to check the work of a junior associate, so do you have to check the work generated by AI,” Owoc said via email.
qs.a: People Are Using ChatGPT as a Lawyer in Court. Some Are Winning. · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: The curated sources from regulators, courts and professional bodies collectively accept the proposition’s core copilot model and materially develop it into operational rules for legal practice and judicial administration. Their common reasoning is that probabilistic, persuasive output can fabricate or misstate authorities, omit relevant issues, import stale or foreign law, and encourage overreliance; therefore qualified humans must independently verify outputs against authoritative sources while retaining judgment, supervision and accountability. These sources extend the proposition through task-specific permissions and prohibitions, confidentiality and bias controls, correction duties, billing rules, approved-tool policies, training requirements and sanctions consequences. Several also substantiate the proposition’s concern about verification costs by describing burdens shifted to courts and opposing parties or requiring task-by-task assessment of whether AI saves time after checking. Material variation concerns implementation rather than the core principle: some permit drafting, summarisation and closed-corpus review subject to safeguards, while others reject current general-purpose tools for legal briefing or unfamiliar research; disclosure ranges from context-dependent or unnecessary unless requested to mandatory certification and identification of AI-assisted passages. Access-to-justice sources favour cautious innovation but stress that self-represented users may lack verification capacity. A smaller strand emphasises benchmarked task performance, affordability or sector transformation, but these broader benefits are generally reported as task-specific findings, possibilities or predictions rather than evidence of consistently improved legal quality. One risk-outlook source does not address verification sufficiently to establish a position, but this does not alter the professional voice’s overall constructive extension of the proposition.

qs.q: VERIFICATION REQUIREMENT  7.1 Content produced using AI must be verified with meaningful human control.

vlens.an: The anonymous frontline-practitioner material supports the proposition’s copilot and verification-cost framing. Its clearest practice-based contribution is that AI can save time on routine duplication and summarisation, but only if a knowledgeable human reviews and adapts the output. The embedded court guidance reinforces that AI use remains governed by existing professional duties and may be inappropriate or require transparency in some contexts. There is material internal variation within the thread: separate posters defend willingness-to-pay pricing and predict major job and fee disruption, but neither claim directly challenges the proposition, and the disruption forecast is unsupported by evidence. Because this is a collection of distinct anonymous comments rather than a unified practitioner position, it should not be treated as representative of frontline practitioners generally.

vlens.an: The selected in-house counsel source supports the proposition that legal AI’s practical value lies in a copilot model constrained by verification costs. It reports rapid production of usable first drafts, supporting task-specific speed and drafting utility, but offers personal experience rather than systematic evidence of consistent quality or net cost savings. Its central reason for support is that polished output may contain fabricated answers and citations, so lawyers must independently review legal analysis and writing and retain professional responsibility. The source consequently favours informed, vigilant adoption rather than either autonomous reliance or avoidance. Its principal variation from the broader synthesis is emphasis: it adds practical concerns about professional duties, intellectual property and then-current technical limits, while giving less attention to whether verification time erodes efficiency gains. Those capability limits are time-specific and should not be treated as current assessments. Because this is one curated in-house perspective, it does not establish the prevalence of these views among in-house counsel or legal operations professionals.

qs.q: It won’t replace me (for a long while anyway, if ever) but it clearly can be a very useful tool when used properly.

vlens.an: The selected professional-liability insurer sources support the proposition’s cautious copilot model. Both accept that AI can assist legal work while treating lawyers and firms as responsible for controlling the resulting risks through human review, training, policies and other safeguards. Their shared reasoning is liability-focused: incorrect output, inadequate oversight and mishandling of confidential information can expose firms to malpractice or related claims, so adoption should be governed rather than autonomous. There is material variation in emphasis. Ames & Gough concentrates on confidentiality, cybersecurity and the continuing application of privilege and work-product protections, while “Law firm AI: insurance considerations” places greater emphasis on checking outputs, implementation controls and fabricated authorities exemplified by Mata v. Avianca. These sources reinforce the cluster’s governance conclusions but provide qualitative risk analysis rather than comparative evidence that benefits are stronger for speed and cost than for quality; nor do they resolve whether verification costs erase efficiency gains. Given the curated evidence, this position applies to these sources and should not be generalized to professional-liability insurers as a whole.

qs.q: Attorney-client privilege and  work product protections still apply for data processed by AI, so lawyers must  maintain confidentiality and prevent improper disclosure.
qs.a: Law Firms Navigate Unrelenting Challenges of Lateral Movement, Cyber Threats, AI Risks and Fraud — Ames & Gough 2024 LPLI Claims Survey (14th annual) · Liability insurers · 2024

elens.an:
The curated 2023–2024 sources collectively support the proposition’s legal-copilot framing. Across judicial guidance, ethics opinions, commentary and early practical demonstrations, the recurring position is that generative AI can accelerate drafting, summarisation, research and administration, but humans retain judgment, supervision and accountability. The common reasons are probabilistic generation, plausible fabrication, stale or foreign law, incomplete analysis and weak contextual understanding; verification must therefore use qualified reviewers and authoritative external sources. Several sources also identify confidentiality, bias, evidence integrity and billing as risks distinct from output accuracy.

The period’s evidence is strongest on the existence of useful assistance, verification duties and concrete harms from failed checking, including the hallucination cases. It is materially weaker on the proposition’s empirical economics: most efficiency and access-to-justice benefits are examples, personal demonstrations or predictions rather than controlled measurements, and only a few sources directly ask whether review creates net savings. This supports, rather than disproves, the synthesis’s caution that speed and cost evidence is stronger than evidence of consistently improved legal quality.

There is meaningful internal variation. Some sources encourage broad but safeguarded adoption and even anticipate future competence duties to use AI; others exclude current legal briefing, case-specific advice or judicial decision-making. Courts and commentators disagree over routine disclosure, accuracy certificates and outright prohibitions, despite agreeing that responsibility remains human. Access-to-justice sources balance scalable assistance against self-represented users’ limited verification capacity and possible transfer of checking costs to courts. Some distinguish purpose-built or closed-corpus tools from general-purpose systems, while Al-Hamim expressly reserves judgment on legal-specific tools; a more optimistic market report does not address verification sufficiently to establish a position. Teaching Law in the Age of Generative AI materially extends the copilot account into education by proposing process-based assessment and independent first attempts. These variations concern implementation and evidential strength, not the period’s overall acceptance of selective, human-supervised use. Because the corpus is curated, this alignment should not be treated as evidence of prevalence among courts, regulators, lawyers or other groups.

elens.an: Across this curated 2025 set, the sources accept the synthesis’s principal proposition and materially develop it into an account of adoption under operational constraint. Reported benchmarks, pilots and deployments support meaningful gains on selected information-processing tasks—especially summarisation, transcript and document analysis, extraction, chronology generation, contract review and administrative drafting—but do not establish consistently superior quality across legal practice. The year’s court policies, ethics opinions and judgments translate the copilot model into concrete controls: independent verification against authoritative sources, retained human accountability, approved-tool and confidentiality rules, and task-specific permissions or prohibitions for submissions, witness evidence and expert reports. Material internal variation concerns scale and trajectory rather than the core proposition. Some sources predict sector-wide transformation, near-ubiquity or even future malpractice implications for non-use; others report that broad workflow adoption remains uncommon or treat access-to-justice benefits as exploratory. Sources also differ on whether verification still leaves net savings: studies and pilots report large task-specific speed or cost gains, while reliability research and sanctions cases show that proposition-by-proposition checking can erode those gains or shift costs to courts and opposing parties. Further contributions identify verification drift, inexperienced lawyers’ evaluative limits, client-supplied AI risks and jurisdiction-specific governance. These records do not show a uniform 2025 consensus or measure prevalence among legal professionals; one Brazilian-courts study documents adoption and governance gaps without resolving the proposition’s verification-cost question.

The curated 2026 sources strongly support the proposition that legal AI’s practical value is defined by qualified human verification and is best understood through a copilot rather than autopilot model. Across professional guidance, court rules, judicial accounts, reported sanctions and commentary, the common reasoning is that generative systems remain probabilistic: they can fabricate authorities, misstate genuine law, omit material issues, import unsuitable jurisdictions and produce biased or misleading outputs. Lawyers, court users and judges therefore retain judgment, supervision and accountability; newer guidance extends this principle expressly to agentic systems and often adds confidentiality, evidence-integrity, disclosure, billing, training and governance controls.

The period also supports the proposition’s distinction between efficiency and quality. The clearest research-oriented source reports faster legal-task completion but mixed quality effects and argues that net time to an acceptable quality threshold is more practically relevant than raw speed. Other sources describe productivity benefits or anticipated efficiencies but generally provide guidance, qualitative experience, survey attitudes, anecdotal incidents or predictions rather than measured net gains after verification.

Material variation concerns degree and application, not the core position. Some sources emphasise selective lower-risk adoption, secure staff-facing pilots and legal-specific grounding; others focus on sanctions, professional development and the risk that persuasive output weakens evaluative skills. Judicial and access-to-justice sources recognise possible benefits for self-represented litigants while warning that users unable to verify outputs may generate meritless filings or shift costs to courts and opponents. Disclosure and certification approaches remain jurisdiction-specific, and one court decision distinguishes fabricated citations from the separate question whether an appeal was frivolous. No inference about prevalence should be drawn from the number of aligned sources in this curated selection.
